## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Brahmadattajātaka* (Ja 323; referred to in some modern studies as the *Brahma Jātaka*) is a canonical verse narrative in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Nārada 2008]. In the commentary's framing story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha relates the account while staying at the Aggāḷava shrine near Āḷavī concerning the monastic regulation on building cells or huts (*kuṭikārasikkhāpada*), noting that the background narrative is explained under the earlier *Maṇikaṇṭhajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The text opens with the verse lemma *Dvayaṁ yācanako ti* [Fausböll 1883].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic living in the park of a king who visited him daily and looked after his needs [Nārada 2008; Ānandajoti 2010]. Although desiring only a simple pair of shoes (or sandals) and a leaf parasol, he refrained for twelve years from asking because he considered begging distressing, humiliating, and destructive of affection [Nārada 2008; Ānandajoti 2010]. Eventually, he voiced his modest request, received the items, and departed; the story is cited in modern studies to illustrate the Bodhisatta's virtue of contentment and profound hesitation to solicit gifts [Nārada 2008; Ānandajoti 2010].
Regarding parallels and text reuse, SuttaCentral lists no direct external canonical parallels, though it records four translations in four languages [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse with the prose *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (volume 3), encompassing four matching segments (790 characters total, with verses §1.1–3.4 corresponding to commentary text at §603_15–612 with 0.91 similarity) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects no cross-language matches in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora [DharmaNexus].
